repairs.before: Which part of the Pod API is extended to report the resources that have actually been applied to a pod and its containers? (answer: PodStatus)
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-01-q1", "brief_id": "rfc-01", "q": "Which kinds of workloads does the proposal say bear the real cost of today's recreate-to-resize behaviour, and which kind mostly tolerates it?", "answer": "Low-replica services, stateful workloads and batch jobs pay in lower availability or higher cost; stateless workloads are generally designed to withstand the disruption", "accept": ["stateful, batch and low-replica workloads suffer; stateless ones tolerate recreation", "low replica count services, stateful workloads, batch jobs; stateless workloads mostly cope", "stateless survives recreation, but stateful/batch/low-replica pay in availability or cost", "sensitive ones are low-replica, stateful and batch; many stateless workloads withstand it"]}
repairs.rationale: The old question was answerable two ways with nothing read (spec=desired/status=observed is a published API convention, and status.containerStatuses[].resources is public surface). Replaced with the brief's who_is_hurt fact, which names a specific three-way population split (low-replica services, stateful, batch) against stateless -- a distinction stated in this brief's material, not derivable from the Kubernetes API convention. Verified against corpus/text/kep-1287-in-place-update-pod-resources.txt lines 173-177. The core_api_idea (PodStatus) fact is now uncovered by design; it was the free one.

repairs.before: Why does the existing CRI UpdateContainerResources call fail to serve Windows and other non-Linux runtimes?

How prescriptive does it intend that definition to be?", "answer": "Only a high-level guide -- defining a detailed or specific way to implement these functions is an explicit non-goal, and implementation specifics are left to each runtime within the bounds of the expected behaviour", "accept": ["a high level guide only; implementation details left to each runtime", "high-level guidance, not a detailed implementation spec", "it is a non-goal to specify how to implement it; runtimes decide the specifics", "broad expected behaviour, with the how left to the runtime"]}

This is a decision the KEP takes, not a property of CRI a model can recall: nothing in the question implies whether the answer is 'a detailed conformance spec' or 'a high-level guide'. Verified at kep-1287 lines 227-230.

repairs.rationale: The old question was a two-way guess on a public namespace (cpu manager none|static, memory manager None|Static), so priors alone win it. Replaced with the brief's cri_gap_readback fact, which requires reading the brief's enumeration of the three CRI gaps and picking out the one about discovery. The answer names a specific missing capability (read back CPU and memory limits currently configured) rather than selecting from a two-item public set. Verified at kep-1287 lines 188-189 and 204-208.

repairs.before: When the systemd cgroup driver is used, how is a container's CPU quota adjusted relative to what the kubelet asked for? (answer: rounded up to the nearest 10ms)
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-02-q2", "brief_id": "rfc-02", "q": "The kubelet cannot decide whether a resize is needed by comparing desired resources against the container's actual configuration. What three causes of legitimate divergence does the design give?", "answer": "Linux kernel enforced minimums for CPU shares and quota, the systemd cgroup driver rounding CPU quota up to the nearest 10ms, and NRI plugins changing the resource configuration", "accept": ["kernel minimums on CPU shares/quota, systemd rounding CPU quota up to 10ms, NRI plugins rewriting the config", "Linux kernel minimums; systemd cgroup driver quota rounding; NRI plugin changes", "kernel-enforced minimums, systemd cgroup driver rounding, NRI plugins", "kernel floors for shares and quota, systemd quota rounding, and NRI plugins altering resources"]}
repairs.rationale: The bare 10ms rounding is a systemd property a model recalls without reading. Rewritten so the unit of credit is the three-item enumeration this brief gives for why a level-triggered comparison is unsound; the 10ms survives only as one member of a list whose other members (kernel-enforced minimums on shares and quota, NRI plugins) are this document's specific claim -- no accept string scores on the number alone. Verified at kep-1287 lines 842-849. No overlap with q1, which asks what 'actuated' means rather than why the kubelet needs it.

repairs.before: What happens when a memory limit is lowered below a container's current usage, on cgroups v1 versus cgroups v2?
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-02-q4", "brief_id": "rfc-02", "q": "A resize request that the runtime does not accept -- how often does the kubelet retry it, and when does it stop?", "answer": "It retries on every subsequent pod sync, until the resize succeeds or the container is terminated", "accept": ["retried on every following pod sync until success or container termination", "every pod sync, until it succeeds or the container terminates", "kubelet keeps retrying each sync; stops on success or when the container is gone", "on each subsequent sync, indefinitely, until success or the container goes away"]}
repairs.rationale: Documented kernel behaviour (v1 rejects the write, v2 OOM-kills) is recallable cold, as the critic's own cold answer shows. Replaced with the brief's retry_policy fact: the retry cadence (every subsequent pod sync) and both termination conditions are kubelet design choices stated only in this material -- a model has no prior telling it whether the retry is backed off, bounded, or per-sync. Verified at kep-1287 lines 862-863. No sibling question covers retry.

repairs.before: Which containerd release first shipped support for the CRI changes this feature depends on? (answer: containerd 1.6.9)
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-03-q1", "brief_id": "rfc-03", "q": "An older client that knows nothing about the ResizePolicy fields sends a pod update. What does it put in those fields, and what does the API server do about it?", "answer": "It sets them to nil, and the API server mutates the update by copying the non-nil values from the old pod into the current one", "accept": ["nil fields; API server copies non-nil values forward from the old pod", "sets ResizePolicy to nil, and the API server carries the old pod's non-nil values over", "they arrive nil and are back-filled from the existing pod by the API server", "nil on the wire; existing non-nil values are preserved by API server mutation"]}
repairs.rationale: A version literal from a heavily indexed public document is pure recall. Replaced with the brief's old_client_handling fact, which requires two specific behaviours to be read: the client writes nil, and the API server repairs the update by copying non-nil values forward from the old pod. Neither half is guessable -- the alternative designs (reject the update, or accept the nil as a clear) are equally plausible priors. Verified at kep-1287 lines 1438-1440. Distinct from q2 (proxy signal), q3 (pre-1.31 restart), q4 (admission with no running containers) and q5 (empty {}).

repairs.before: How much swap is available to Kubernetes workloads by default under the new kubelet configuration knob? (answer: Zero)

repairs.before: Why is setting swappiness listed as a non-goal?

What does that deferral make swap, within the scope of this one?", "answer": "An overcommitted resource -- nothing accounts for swap per workload here, and there is no API for controlling how limits are computed", "accept": ["an overcommitted resource", "swap is overcommitted in this KEP", "overcommitted, since nothing accounts for it per workload", "it becomes an overcommitted resource for the scope of this proposal"]}
repairs.rationale: vm.swappiness is a global sysctl, so 'it is already settable system-wide' is free; the question's own shape left no other answer. That consequence is a stated conclusion, not a property of Linux: a model with no access to this material has no basis to say whether swap is overcommitted, reserved, or simply unavailable. Verified at kep-2400 lines 193-198.

repairs.before: How is ContainerMemoryProportion calculated? (accept included the loose 'request over node memory')
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-05-q1", "brief_id": "rfc-05", "q": "ContainerMemoryProportion is a ratio of one container-level quantity to one node-level quantity. Name both precisely.", "answer": "The container's memory request, divided by the node's total physical memory (not its allocatable memory)", "accept": ["container memory request / node total physical memory", "the memory request of the container over the node's total physical memory", "request (not limit) divided by the node's physical memory total", "memory request divided by total physical memory of the node"]}
repairs.rationale: The variable name decomposes to the formula, so the old accept[2] 'request over node memory' was free. The two discriminators that require reading are request-not-limit and total-physical-not-allocatable -- allocatable is the value every other kubelet calculation uses, so a cold model that guesses from the name lands on the wrong denominator. The question now demands both quantities precisely and the accept list no longer sanctions the vague form. Verified at kep-2400 line 292. Question shape deliberately avoids offering the alternatives, which would turn it into a four-way multiple choice.

repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-05-q4", "brief_id": "rfc-05", "q": "In the worked example, what swap limits do containers A and B end up with?", "answer": "Container A gets 19 GB and container B gets 9.5 GB", "accept": ["19G and 9.5G", "A: 19 GB, B: 9.5 GB", "19 GB and 9.5 GB", "0.5 x 38G = 19G and 0.25 x 38G = 9.5G"]}
repairs.rationale: Grading-key unit slip only; the arithmetic is right and untouched. 19 GiB = 19 * 1024^3 / 1e9 = 20.401 GB, which is 7.37% larger than the 19 GB the brief derives, so accept[2] '19 GiB / 9.5 GiB' sanctioned a numerically different answer as correct. The brief states 40 GB memory, 40 GB swap, 2 GB system-reserved, and the source states `0.5 * 38G` = `19G` (kep-2400 lines 305-312) -- all GB. Replaced the GiB variant with a plain-GB variant; question and canonical answer unchanged.

repairs.before: Encrypted swap is named as the mitigation for the security risk, so why doesn't the KEP implement it?
repairs.after: {"id": "rfc-06-q2", "brief_id": "rfc-06", "q": "Which volumes does Kubernetes guarantee will never have their memory land on disk, and what does the kubelet do to keep that guarantee once swap is permitted on the node?", "answer": "Secrets and memory-backed emptyDirs, which the kubelet mounts as tmpfs on the host; when --fail-swap-on=false it uses the tmpfs noswap option so those pages cannot swap out", "accept": ["Secrets and memory-backed emptyDirs; mounted as tmpfs with the noswap option when --fail-swap-on=false", "secret volumes and memory-backed emptyDir; kubelet uses tmpfs noswap to keep their pages off disk", "tmpfs-mounted volumes such as Secrets and memory-backed emptyDirs, protected with the tmpfs noswap mount option", "Secrets and memory-backed emptyDirs, mounted tmpfs and given noswap so they never reach disk"]}
repairs.rationale: The old question handed over the mitigation and asked why a kubelet KEP does not implement an OS-level thing -- scope is the only answer shape available, so it graded question-reading rather than comprehension. Replaced with the brief's memory_backed_guarantee and noswap_mitigation facts. The required answer pairs a named guarantee (Secrets, memory-backed emptyDirs) with the specific mechanism and its precondition (tmpfs mount, noswap option, gated on --fail-swap-on=false); the mechanism half cannot be produced from the question. Verified at kep-2400 lines 507-511. Distinct from q3 (when the detection is retired) and q4 (what happens on an old kernel).
